title: Salman Khan’s Most Praised Film Can’t Get Released — Because India’s Censors Won’t Say Yes or No
excerpt: The CBFC has withheld certification for Maatrubhumi, the Galwan Valley war drama that filmmakers loved and diplomats fear
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Salman Khan's film *Maatrubhumi* faces certification delays from India's censors.
  • The film, inspired by the Galwan Valley clash, has been renamed and recut multiple times.
  • CBFC has not rejected the film but has withheld certification without explanation.
  • Industry insiders praise *Maatrubhumi* for its serious treatment of the Galwan incident.
  • The film's release is crucial for the Indian diaspora, resonating with their national security concerns.
Maatrubhumi's Certification Saga
›Original title: *Battle of Galwan*
›Renamed to *Maatrubhumi* to lower diplomatic tensions.
›Initially planned release: April (Eid), now delayed.
›Current status: Certification withheld by CBFC.
The most politically charged film in Bollywood right now just hit another wall — and this time, it's India's own censors putting up the roadblock. **Salman Khan's** *Maatrubhumi*, the war drama inspired by the 2020 Galwan Valley clash between Indian and Chinese troops, has had its certification withheld by the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC), according to an NDTV report. The move casts fresh doubt over a film that has already been renamed, recut, and delayed twice — and may now miss its third planned release window. If you've been following this saga, you know the backstory reads like a thriller in its own right. The film was originally titled *Battle of Galwan* — a name so blunt it practically dared the world to take sides. Chinese social media erupted. Users on Weibo accused the project of misrepresenting the border clash that killed 20 Indian soldiers and an undisclosed number of Chinese troops in June 2020. India's Ministry of External Affairs was forced to weigh in, with spokesperson **Randhir Jaiswal** carefully distancing the government: "MEA has no role in this or such ventures." The makers blinked first. *Battle of Galwan* became *Maatrubhumi* — Motherland — a softer, more abstract title designed to lower the diplomatic temperature. Changes were made to the film itself. An April release timed to Eid was scrapped. An August slot around Independence Day was quietly penciled in. And now, even that appears to be slipping away. ## The Silence That Speaks Here's what makes this particularly strange: the CBFC hasn't rejected the film. It hasn't demanded specific cuts. It has simply... withheld the certificate. No clearance, no rejection, just bureaucratic silence. For a film starring the biggest mass star in Hindi cinema, produced by his own banner **Salman Khan Films**, and directed by **Apoorva Lakhia**, that kind of limbo sends a very specific signal. The whisper in trade circles is that the film's subject matter — a detailed recreation of the Galwan Valley confrontation, with Salman playing **Colonel Santosh Babu**, the commanding officer who led the 16 Bihar Regiment during the standoff — makes it diplomatically radioactive. India has spent years carefully managing the bilateral relationship with China through quiet disengagement talks and deliberate ambiguity. A big-budget Bollywood spectacle charging through all of that is not something anyone in South Block seems eager to greenlight. ## The Irony
Industry Buzz Around Maatrubhumi
›Top filmmakers praised the film after a rough cut screening.
›Subhash Ghai: 'A must-watch.'
›Kabir Khan: Moved by the film's portrayal.
›Chitrangda Singh stars as the female lead.
And yet — this is the delicious part — the people who have actually seen the film cannot stop praising it. When Salman screened a rough cut for a group of top filmmakers earlier this year, the response was electric. **Subhash Ghai** called it a must-watch. **Kabir Khan** — a man who knows a thing or two about military dramas — was reportedly moved. The word from inside the industry is that *Maatrubhumi* treats the Galwan incident with genuine gravity and restraint, not jingoistic spectacle. **Chitrangda Singh** plays the female lead, with **Himesh Reshammiya** handling the music — an unexpected but intriguing choice for a war drama. The teaser, unveiled on December 27, 2025 (Salman's 60th birthday), generated immediate buzz. By all accounts, the film is ready to go.## What the Diaspora Is Losing For the Indian diaspora — especially in the US, UK, and Canada — the Galwan clash remains one of the most emotionally resonant national security events of the decade. The bravery of Colonel Santosh Babu, who was posthumously awarded the Maha Vir Chakra, is a story families across the diaspora know and honour. A film about it, starring Salman Khan, would be appointment viewing in NRI households from New Jersey to Southall.
Cultural Impact on the Diaspora
›Galwan clash: Key national security event for the diaspora.
›Colonel Santosh Babu: Honored with the Maha Vir Chakra.
›Film would resonate with NRI audiences in US, UK, Canada.
›Bollywood's irony: Patriotic films thrive, real stories face barriers.
Instead, it's sitting on a government shelf.For an industry that has spent years wrapping itself in the tricolour — from *Uri* to *Border 2* to Dhurandhar — the irony is almost too perfect. Bollywood can make patriotic films about fictional wars all day long. But the moment it tries to tell the story of a real one, the doors close. The question now is whether the CBFC's hesitation is temporary — a matter of bureaucratic timing ahead of the next round of border talks — or something more permanent. Either way, Salman Khan's most personal, most praised, most dangerous film is still waiting for permission to exist.
